summary: The note describes local public health campaigns launched since September 2023 to fight sedentary lifestyles, led by the "Awakening the Sedentary Society" campaign. It covers barrier-busting workshops, the "Move More" app, school and workplace programs, community challenges, and inclusivity efforts. Experts stress that small, consistent increases in movement bring major health benefits.
one_line: Local public health initiatives since late 2023 promote everyday movement through campaigns, an app, school programs, workplace changes, community events and accessible fitness.
key_facts: The "Awakening the Sedentary Society" campaign kicked off on October 3, 2023, to bring inactivity to the forefront of the community's health dialogue.
Dr. Emily Torres, an epidemiologist and public health advocate, said "a sedentary lifestyle is the new smoking."
Risks of inactivity named in the note include heart disease, diabetes, obesity, and mental health disorders.
A public health department survey released on November 15, 2023, found the top reasons for not exercising are lack of time, lack of motivation, and lack of access to facilities.
Fitness expert Lucas Bennett has run community workshops since the start of December 2023 offering time-management tips, motivational techniques, and exercises needing no special equipment.

The "Move More" smartphone app, built with the health department and app developers, reminds users to stand, stretch, or walk; it launched January 10, 2024, and has been downloaded over 100,000 times.
The "Active Classrooms" project started in February 2024, introducing mandatory movement breaks and physical activity in lesson plans.
Primary School Teacher Anna Johnson reported that "Active Spellings" (jumping jacks while spelling words) improved children's activity, concentration, and engagement.
The "10,000 Steps Challenge" took place on March 5, 2024, and participants collectively walked more than 50 million steps.
Workplaces are adopting standing desks, treadmill workstations, and lunch hour walking groups, linked to higher productivity and fewer sick days.
Corporate Wellness Consultant Michael Reed said "Investing in your employees' health is investing in your company's success."
Adaptive fitness programs serve people of differing abilities and ages; wheelchair athlete Sandra Kim is a vocal supporter.
Lucas Bennett recommends a mix of cardiovascular exercise, strength training, and flexibility work, with the mantra "Consistency over intensity."
